title: If AI Writes the Code, What Does the Developer Do?
author: ia-bin
selftext:
Quick note: English isn’t my first language, so I used AI to polish the writing. The ideas, examples, and experiences below are my own.



Yesterday I posted about AI game development and got a lot of pushback, especially around one question:

If AI is writing the code, what exactly am I doing?

Fair question.

My first game, iaBrick, was built the old-fashioned way. I learned Swift from scratch and wrote the code myself, line by line. It took me close to a year.

And I’m glad I did it.

But a lot of that year was spent fighting things I honestly didn’t care much about: networking bugs, file handling, UI state, backend communication, login logic, random crashes, framework quirks, etc.

Then I started building iaReveal with AI doing much more of the implementation.

And I had a slightly uncomfortable realization:

For a lot of standard infrastructure code, AI is simply better than I am.

So why am I insisting on writing a worse version myself?

I sometimes think of AI as another abstraction layer in programming.

People moved from machine code to assembly, then C, C++, frameworks, engines, visual tools, etc. Nobody says using Unity means you “didn’t make the game” because you didn’t write the renderer from scratch.

AI feels like the next step. Not literally a programming language, obviously, but increasingly I describe what the system must do instead of manually writing every step of how it does it.

But this is also where I think the whole “one prompt = one game” idea gets misleading.

If you want to make something based on an existing game structure — a platformer, shooter, match-3, survival game, familiar puzzle, whatever — then yes, I can absolutely imagine AI getting closer and closer to “one prompt development.”

The mechanics already exist.

There are examples everywhere.

AI mostly has to reproduce a known structure, then change the art, story, theme, characters or presentation.

But if the mechanic itself is new, that stops working very quickly.

You can’t just say:

“Make me a completely new puzzle game that nobody has made before.”

What exactly should the AI build?

There is no existing mechanic to copy.

No established state model.

No known solvability rules.

No proven generator.

No standard optimization strategy.

Someone still has to work those things out.

And that is where most of my actual work has moved.

I spend a lot less time typing syntax now, but much more time thinking about questions like:

•	What exactly is the mechanic?

•	What makes a move interesting rather than arbitrary?

•	What states must never happen?

•	Can procedurally generated boards always be solved?

•	Is “technically solvable” actually playable?

•	Can a board be solvable but still strategically doomed for a normal player?

•	How should new states be generated without breaking the rules?

•	How much search can I afford during initialization?

•	How do I make generation fast enough that the player doesn’t think the app froze?

•	What happens when two mechanics interact in some edge case I didn’t anticipate?

Once I can answer those questions clearly, AI is often very good at turning the answers into code.

But AI cannot save me from having to answer them.

That’s the difference I care about.

“Make another version of a known game” may increasingly become close to a one-prompt problem.

“Invent a new game mechanic and make it robust enough for a commercial game” is a very different problem.

And honestly, that second problem is the part I enjoy.

Some people love coding itself. Some people love debugging. Totally fair.

My fun is different.

I like taking a game mechanic that exists only in my head, finding out why the first version doesn’t work, fixing the logic, and eventually seeing someone else play it.

I also have more puzzle-game ideas than I have patience to spend 6–12 months coding each one by hand.

AI lets me try more of them.

And yes, I’d also like the games to make money eventually.

I don’t really see why that should be embarrassing either.

If players don’t like the game, AI doesn’t magically make them pay for it.

You can build ten bad games ten times faster and still have ten bad games.

So I no longer think “who typed the code?” is the most interesting question.

For me the more interesting question is:

who figured out what the game should actually be, and how to make that idea work?

That’s the part I still want to own.





P.S. If you’re wondering why I still haven’t officially released the iOS version of iaBrick, but did officially release the iOS version of iaReveal first, this is a big part of the reason. AI later helped me fix most of iaBrick’s crash bugs, and I almost never see crashes now — but debugging that codebase honestly left me a little traumatized. I still keep worrying that somewhere in my own old spaghetti code there’s a fatal bug waiting to ruin the player experience. So I’m still torn between keeping that original codebase alive vs. just letting AI help me rewrite the whole game cleanly from scratch. Ironically, the HTML demo version of iaBrick that I had AI help build and put on [itch.io](http://itch.io) has been running without any fatal bugs so far — actually, I haven’t even run into a minor bug yet.
